section.title: The Lord's Supper
section.sectionRationale: Paul turns from head coverings to a graver failure at the very table meant to unite the church. Their gatherings do more harm than good: the well fed shame the poor, and so what they eat is not really the Lord's Supper at all. Into this disorder Paul hands on the words of institution he received from the Lord, and calls each believer to examine himself and discern the body, lest the meal of grace become a meal of judgment.
section.thesis: The Lord's Supper proclaims Christ's death for us until He comes, so a church that shames the poor at that table has forgotten the cross; each believer must examine himself and discern the body, receiving the meal as the sign of the new covenant in Christ's blood, not as an occasion for division and judgment.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the rebuke, their divisions turn the supper into something that is not the Lord's Supper; the tradition received from the Lord, this is My body, the new covenant in My blood, proclaim His death until He comes; and the examination, discern the body, or you eat and drink judgment.

verses.text: In the following instructions I have no praise to offer, because your gatherings do more harm than good.
First of all, I hear that when you come together as a church, there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it.
And indeed, there must be differences among you to show which of you are approved.
Now then, when you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat.
For as you eat, each of you goes ahead without sharing his meal. While one remains hungry, another gets drunk.
Don’t you have your own homes in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What can I say to you? Shall I praise you for this? No, I will not!

units.label: The tradition received from the Lord
units.note: this is My body, the new covenant in My blood

verses.text: For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you: The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread,
and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, “This is My {{soma|body}}, which is for you; do this in {{anamnesis|remembrance}} of Me.”
In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new {{diatheke|covenant}} in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.”
For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.

units.label: Examine and discern the body
units.note: or you eat and drink judgment

verses.text: Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord.
Each one must {{dokimazo|examine}} himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup.
For anyone who eats and drinks without {{diakrino|recognizing}} the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a number of you have fallen asleep.
Now if we judged ourselves properly, we would not come under judgment.
But when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world.
So, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.
If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that when you come together it will not result in judgment. And when I come, I will give instructions about the remaining matters.

soma.gloss: Body. At the table Jesus calls the bread His body, given for us, and Paul uses the same word for sinning against the body and blood of the Lord and for failing to discern the body. It carries a double weight in this passage: the crucified body of Christ, and the church which is His body, so that despising the poor is treated as an offense against the Lord Himself.

anamnesis.gloss: Remembrance, a calling to mind that makes a past event present and active. Do this in remembrance of Me is more than nostalgia; it is a covenant memorial in which the church proclaims and lays hold of Christ's finished death, echoing the way Israel remembered the Passover deliverance.

diatheke.gloss: Covenant, a binding arrangement God graciously establishes. The cup is the new covenant in Christ's blood, fulfilling the promise of Jeremiah 31 of a covenant written on the heart with sins forgiven. The word points beyond a shared meal to the whole new relationship purchased at the cross.

dokimazo.gloss: To examine, test, and approve after scrutiny. Each one must examine himself before eating, not to earn a place at the table but to come honestly, repentant, and in love toward the body, so that the meal is received rightly rather than carelessly.

diakrino.gloss: To distinguish, discern, judge rightly between things. To eat without recognizing the body is to fail to discern what the meal is and who the church is, treating the Supper as common food and the poor brother as nothing; such careless eating brings judgment rather than blessing.

basic.context: The Corinthians came together for a shared meal that included the Lord's Supper, but their gatherings had become a display of the same divisions that ran through the whole letter. The rich ate their fill and even got drunk while the poor went hungry and were shamed. Paul says that when they eat like this it is not really the Lord's Supper at all. He reminds them of the words Jesus spoke on the night He was betrayed, and warns that to eat carelessly, without discerning the body, is to eat and drink judgment.
basic.hermeneutics: This is correction of a specific abuse, not a full theology of the sacrament, though it teaches us much. Paul grounds his rebuke in the tradition he received from the Lord, the words of institution, and applies it pastorally: examine yourself, wait for one another, and if you are only hungry, eat at home. The abiding truths are the meaning of the Supper and the call to receive it worthily.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus calls the bread His soma, His body, given for us, and the same word returns when Paul warns against sinning against the body and failing to discern the body. The Supper is done in anamnesis, remembrance, a living memorial that proclaims His death. The cup is the new diatheke, covenant, in His blood. So each believer must dokimazo, examine himself, and diakrino, discern the body, rather than eat carelessly.
basic.typology: The Supper fulfills the Passover: as Israel remembered its rescue from Egypt with a meal, the church remembers a greater rescue, for Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. The new covenant in His blood fulfills Jeremiah's promise of a covenant with sins forgiven, sealed not with the blood of bulls but with the blood of the Lord.
basic.christ: Christ stands at the center of the table. It is His body given and His blood poured out that the bread and cup proclaim. The Supper looks back to His death for us on the cross and forward to His return, for we eat and drink until He comes. He is both the host who gives the meal and the sacrifice the meal proclaims.
basic.god: God is not mocked at His own table. He disciplines a careless church, even with weakness, sickness, and death, yet He does so as a Father, so that His people will not be condemned with the world. His judgment here is corrective mercy, aimed at bringing the church back to love and to the cross.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 22 records the same words of institution at the Last Supper. Exodus 12 gives the Passover the Supper fulfills. Jeremiah 31 promises the new covenant sealed in Christ's blood. 1 Corinthians 10 says the cup and bread are a participation in the blood and body of Christ.
basic.oneStory: From the Passover in Egypt to the new covenant promised by the prophets, God's rescue has always been marked by a meal. At the cross the true Lamb is slain, and the church now proclaims His death in bread and cup until He comes again to share the feast of the kingdom. The Lord's Supper is a hinge between what Christ has done and what He will yet do.

context.literary:
The unit is held together by a ring of repeated words. Paul says come together in verses 17, 18, 20, 33 and 34, so the whole section is about what happens when the church gathers. Praise gives a second frame: he commended them in verse 2, has no praise in verse 17, and asks in verse 22 whether he should praise them for this, with a flat no. In the middle, the words of Jesus in verses 23 to 26 stand like a pillar between a rebuke in verses 17 to 22 and the practical instructions in verses 27 to 34. Paul does not let the story of the Supper be only a reminder. It is the measure by which the meal at Corinth is found wanting.

A cluster of related words carries the argument. Divisions in verse 18 and differences in verse 19 prepare for a family of words about judging. The Corinthians are to examine themselves, verse 28, and to recognize the body, verse 29, and to judge themselves, verse 31, so that they are not judged, verse 32. The same root, krino, runs through verses 29 to 34, and the sentence turns on a deliberate play: judge yourselves now, so that you are not judged later. Verse 19 also plays on a word that returns in verse 28. Those who are approved are known by the testing that sorts a church, and each one must test himself.

The passage sits between the argument over head coverings and the long section on gifts, and it joins them. All three concern the church's assembly, and in each Paul's question is whether the gathering builds the body or harms it, a question stated outright in verse 17: your gatherings do more harm than good.
context.historical:
The Lord's Supper in the first generation was not a small wafer and sip at the end of a service. It was part of a real evening meal, the deipnon, which is why Paul can say after supper in verse 25. Christians met in homes, and the rooms available were limited. Many scholars think that the wealthy host's dining room held only a few guests, who reclined in the formal manner, while others waited in the courtyard, so that status could be arranged by the place one was given. The social habits of the Greek and Roman world make the problem in verse 21 easy to picture. A better supper for the well off and a plainer one for the rest was normal at private dinners, and in the Corinthian house church people brought their own food to a shared table, so that the rich arrived early and finished while slaves and laborers, who could not leave work until evening, came to what was left. Paul says one is hungry and another drunk.

The tradition he cites is an old one. He received it from the Lord and passed it on, verse 23, and he writes about twenty five years after the Last Supper, so this is the earliest written account of its institution. It stands in close agreement with Luke 22:19 and 20, and the same night is told in Matthew 26:26 to 29 and Mark 14:22 to 25. The Last Supper took place in the setting of the Passover, Luke 22:7 to 15, and the early church's memory of it was shaped by that. Corinth also knew sacred meals of its own, and in 10:14 to 22 Paul has already told them that they cannot share the table of the Lord and the table of demons. The Supper here is a table of a different kind: one where status counts for nothing, because all eat from one loaf, 10:17.
context.canonical:
The Supper reaches back to Exodus 12, where Israel ate the Passover lamb on the night of rescue, and to Exodus 24:8, where Moses sprinkled the people with the blood of the covenant and said that it was the covenant the LORD had made. Jesus takes up both when He says this cup is the new covenant in My blood, verse 25, and the new covenant itself is promised in Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, where God says He will forgive their wickedness and remember their sins no more. Paul will say a few chapters earlier that Christ, our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, 1 Corinthians 5:7. The wilderness meals of manna and water appear in 10:1 to 4 as a warning that sharing in holy things does not guarantee approval.

Within the New Testament the Supper has other echoes. In John 6:51 to 58 Jesus calls Himself the bread of life, and the church's gathering around bread in Acts 2:42 and 46 and 20:7 shows that the breaking of bread was a regular part of its life. Jude 12 warns about those who feast at the church's love feasts without reverence, a sign that Corinth's problem was not unique. The Supper also looks forward. Jesus said that He would not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes, Luke 22:18, and the book of Revelation closes the story with the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. Hebrews 9:15 to 22 provides the key to the language of blood and covenant, explaining why a covenant of this kind is established by a death.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is angry and also tender. The failure he names is not first a ritual mistake but a moral one: those who have food take it before those who have none, and the Lord's table is turned into a display of rank. He wants the Corinthians to see that this makes a nonsense of the very thing they claim to be doing. They come together to eat the Lord's Supper, yet verse 20 says that what they eat is not it. The Supper has a meaning laid down by Christ, and meaning cannot be added to or taken from by the habits of those who gather around it.

His correction therefore moves in three steps. He takes them back to the words and acts of Jesus, so that the church is recalled to what it received. He turns that memory into a question for each person, how do I come to this table, and he says that each must examine himself. And then he gives plain, ordinary instructions: wait for one another, and eat at home if you are hungry, verses 33 and 34. The first hearers were meant to understand that the way they treated the poorer members was a way of treating Christ's body, and that the loving, orderly meal was the proof that they had grasped what His death was for. He means to bring them to the table with a humble heart, to correct them before the Lord has to, and to restore the meal as a place where the divisions of the world are set aside.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of the passage describes: it reports what Paul has heard about the meals, what the rich and poor were doing, and what had happened to the congregation in the form of weakness, sickness and death in verse 30. Some of it prescribes: the words of institution, which Paul says he received from the Lord, the instruction to do this in remembrance, the proclamation of the Lord's death until He comes, the call to examine oneself, and the command to wait for one another. A fair test of any application is whether it preserves the proclamation and the love Paul asks for.

There is a danger in both directions. One is to take the warning about eating in an unworthy manner and to turn it into a reason for fear, so that an anxious believer stays away because of sin the Lord has already forgiven. The passage does not say this. Examination is meant to lead to repentance and to the table, not away from it. The other danger is to read the warning lightly. The same chapter tells us that the Lord cares enough about this meal to discipline those who despise His people at it. The weakness and death of verse 30 are what happened to some at Corinth, and the text does not say that every illness is a judgment, so we should not read that into the sickbed of any individual. What carries forward is the call to receive the Supper in faith, in unity, in repentance and with concern for the poor.

debates.question: What does it mean to eat without recognizing the body, verse 29?

views.label: The church as the body of Christ
views.case: The whole chapter is about divisions and the neglect of the poor, and the next chapter turns to the church as the body of Christ, 12:12 to 27. In 10:17 the one loaf means that we, though many, are one body. To fail to recognize the body is to eat without regard to the people beside you.

views.label: The body of Christ given on the cross
views.case: Verse 24 says this is My body, and verse 27 speaks of the body and blood of the Lord. On this view eating without recognizing the body means treating the bread as common food and not seeing the death of Christ it proclaims.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Others say the two senses cannot be separated. The body given for us is the body that makes us one, so to despise the church at the table is to despise what Christ's death was for.

debates.bearing: Whatever reading is chosen, Paul's practical instruction is the same: wait for one another, eat in love, and let the table show what the cross has done, verses 33 and 34.

debates.question: What is an unworthy manner, and what does examining oneself involve?

views.label: A matter of how one eats
views.case: Paul uses an adverb: eats and drinks in an unworthy manner, verse 27. The fault is in the conduct at the meal, which in Corinth meant greed, drunkenness and contempt for the poor. A person is not made unworthy by weakness in faith, only by acting against the meaning of the meal.

views.label: A matter of the person's state
views.case: Some traditions have taught that a person must be free of known unrepented sin, and prepared in a particular way, before coming. They read the call to examine as a call to prepare by confession and, in some practices, to be reconciled with others first, Matthew 5:23 and 24.

views.label: A matter of faith in Christ
views.case: A third emphasis is that the only worthiness is Christ's, and that the unworthy eater is the one who does not trust Him or who treats the meal as a mere ceremony.

debates.bearing: All agree that no one is worthy by himself, and that the call to examine leads to repentance and trust. The warning is for the careless and contemptuous, not for the sorry.

debates.question: In what sense is the bread His body?

views.label: A remembrance and proclamation
views.case: Jesus says do this in remembrance of Me, and Paul says that the Supper proclaims the Lord's death, verses 24 to 26. Zwingli and many Baptist and Free churches take the words as a sign of what Christ has done and a meal of memory and fellowship.

views.label: A real spiritual presence
views.case: Calvin and the Reformed tradition hold that Christ is truly present to the believer by the Spirit, and that those who eat in faith are fed. 1 Corinthians 10:16 asks whether the cup is a participation in the blood of Christ.

views.label: A bodily presence in the elements
views.case: Lutherans hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine, and Roman Catholics hold that the bread and wine are changed into His body and blood. Both appeal to the plain force of this is My body.

debates.bearing: The passage makes certain that the Supper is no empty rite: those who misuse it face real discipline. But it does not itself settle the manner of Christ's presence, and Christians who disagree here can still hold the same table as far as Paul's call to love.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 23 hides a pair of words that English cannot show. Paul says I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you, and then says that Jesus was betrayed that night. Both are forms of the one verb paradidomi, to hand over or hand on. The word is used for what one generation delivers to the next, as in 15:3, and for Judas handing Jesus over. The tradition of the Supper is the thing handed on, and it was instituted on the night of the handing over. The act of betrayal is not the end of the story; the same verb is used of the Father giving up His Son for us in Romans 8:32.

The sin at the meal is named with the verb prolambano in verse 21, each one goes ahead, taking his own supper first, as the BSB footnote shows, literally each takes first his own meal. The Greek word for a meal here is deipnon, the main evening supper, and the phrase in verse 20 that it is not the Lord's Supper uses the adjective kyriakon, belonging to the Lord, so that the supper is the Lord's by ownership as well as by institution. The only other New Testament use of the adjective is the Lord's Day in Revelation 1:10.

Verse 26 says you proclaim the Lord's death, using katangello, to announce publicly, the word used in 9:14 of those who proclaim the gospel. The meal is a form of preaching: even with no one speaking, it announces the death of Christ until He comes.

The warning words need care. Enochos in verse 27, rendered guilty of, is the language of liability, so to be enochos of the body and blood is to be answerable for it. The BSB footnote gives the alternative will be responsible for the. In verse 29 the manuscripts divide: the text reads without recognizing the body, while the footnote notes that some manuscripts, behind the King James Version, read the body of the Lord. Either way the sense is the same. Verse 30 says that many have fallen asleep, from koimao, the familiar New Testament word for death as sleep, as in 15:6 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13. Verse 32 uses paideuo for the Lord's discipline, from the word for a child's training, Hebrews 12:5 to 11, which is why Paul can say that this is discipline so that we will not be condemned with the world. The verbs of judgment, krino, diakrino and katakrino, are related, and their relation is the heart of the argument: the church that judges itself rightly is not subject to condemnation.

typology.type: The Passover lamb and the night of rescue
typology.fulfillment: At the first Passover Israel ate roasted lamb in haste, with its blood on the doorposts, and the LORD passed over, Exodus 12:7 and 13. Paul says plainly that Christ, our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, 1 Corinthians 5:7, and John calls Him the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29. The Supper is the church's Passover meal, remembering a deliverance that is greater because it is from sin and death. The type falls short because the first lamb had to be killed again every year; Christ died once for all, Hebrews 10:10.

After Moses sprinkled the blood of the covenant, Aaron, his sons and seventy elders of Israel went up, saw the God of Israel, and ate and drank, Exodus 24:8 to 11. A covenant sealed with blood was followed by a meal in God's presence. Jesus takes the same shape and speaks of the new covenant in His blood. The escalation is that now every believer, not only the elders, eats and drinks at His table. The type is incomplete because Sinai's covenant was broken by Israel, and Jeremiah 31:31 to 34 looked for one that would be written on the heart.

typology.type: Manna and the water from the rock
typology.fulfillment: In 1 Corinthians 10:3 and 4 Paul says that Israel ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink, for the rock was Christ. In John 6:31 to 35 Jesus says that the bread from heaven is now the One the Father gives. The Supper continues the pattern: God feeds His people on the way. The type is a warning as well, for most of those who ate the manna died in the wilderness, which is the point of 10:5 and of the sober words of 11:30.

typology.type: The feast prepared for all peoples
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 25:6 to 8 pictures the LORD preparing a feast of rich food for all peoples on His mountain, swallowing up death forever and wiping away tears. The Lord's Supper is a foretaste, since we eat until He comes. Revelation 19:9 names the final form: the marriage supper of the Lamb. The type falls short only in that the Supper is partial, and Jesus said He would not drink again of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes, Luke 22:18.

study.christ:
Christ is at once the host, the meal and the one remembered. Paul says that the Lord Jesus took bread, and so the Supper is not the church's invention; He gave it. At it He speaks of My body, which is for you, verse 24, and of the cup that is the new covenant in My blood. The little words for you carry the whole of the gospel. His body was given on behalf of others, not as the victim of events but as one who offered Himself, and the blood is that of the covenant, which makes forgiveness and a new relationship with God possible, Jeremiah 31:34, Hebrews 9:15.

The scene is told with a deep sense of timing. It was the night He was betrayed, when He knew what lay ahead, Luke 22:15, and He chose to give His disciples not an explanation but a meal. Every time the church eats it proclaims the death of the Lord, not a doctrine about it, and the Lord who died is also the Lord who is coming. Until He comes, verse 26, holds the whole of the Christian story between two points, the cross behind and the return ahead, and Christ is both. The bread looks back to the sacrifice, and it looks forward to the day when we will eat with Him in the kingdom, Luke 22:16 and 18.

The Corinthian failure is also a failure to see Christ. The one whose table it is gave Himself up for the poor and made Himself poor for others' sake, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and so to humiliate those who have nothing at this meal is to deny the pattern of the Host. Christ's meals with sinners, Luke 15:2, and His welcome of the poor are the model for the church's table. He is also the one who disciplines. The Lord's judgment in verses 30 to 32 is that of the Lord who loves His church and will not leave it in contempt of itself. We should not make every detail of the meal into a picture of Christ, but the central lines are clear: this meal is about Him, from beginning to end.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who is not mocked at His own table. The Supper is the Lord's, and the weight of Paul's warning rests on that. God takes the way His people treat one another at this meal with great seriousness, because the church is His, bought with the blood of His Son. He sees the hungry person turned away and the rich person who eats his fill, and He regards it as sin against the body and blood of the Lord, verse 27.

At the same time, God's judgment here is the judgment of a Father. Verse 32 is one of the most important lines in the chapter: when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world. Two kinds of judgment are being distinguished. The condemnation of the world is final; the discipline of the church is for correction, and its purpose is rescue. This matches Hebrews 12:5 to 11, where the Lord disciplines those He loves, and Proverbs 3:11 and 12. It also matches Romans 8:1, that there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. The doctrine of God that emerges is one in which holiness and mercy are not set against each other. The God who will not have His table abused is also the God who will not abandon those who abuse it, but corrects them so that they may be saved.

The passage reveals the covenant-keeping character of God, who has bound Himself in a new covenant, and who gives a meal as its sign, as He did at the Passover and at Sinai. It shows His patience, because Paul says if we judged ourselves properly we would not come under judgment, which gives a space for repentance before discipline falls. And it shows His concern for the poor and the despised, those who have nothing, verse 22, whom He will not let be humiliated in His own house.

For worship this means coming with reverence and with joy. It is a reverent meal because He is holy, and a joyful one because He has given His Son. It means being slow to treat anyone as less than a member of the family, since the Father has set one table and one loaf, and examining ourselves in the light of His mercy and not in fear of rejection.

crossReferences.note: Luke's account of the Last Supper is the closest parallel to Paul's. He records the bread given for you and the cup poured out as the new covenant in His blood, and adds that Jesus had earnestly desired to eat this Passover with His disciples. Paul's version is therefore not a later invention but a shared tradition.

The first Passover, with the lamb, the blood on the doorposts and the instruction that it be kept as a memorial. The Supper is the church's counterpart: a meal of rescue, and a command to remember, now fulfilled in the lamb who takes away the sin of the world.

The covenant is ratified with blood, and the elders eat and drink in the presence of God. Jesus' words about the new covenant in My blood recall this scene, and the Supper is a meal where God and His people are again at one table.

The promise of a new covenant that is not like the old, written on the heart, with sins forgiven and remembered no more. Jesus' cup announces its beginning. The Supper is the church's recurring celebration of a covenant already inaugurated.

Christ, our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, so keep the feast with sincerity and truth. Paul has already tied the Passover to Christ and to the holy life of the church, which is what he now applies to the meal at Corinth.

Paul asks whether the cup is a participation in the blood of Christ, and says that we who are many are one body because we share one loaf. This is the best commentary on verse 29, since it shows that the one loaf makes the church one and rules out divisions at the table.

Jesus calls Himself the living bread that came down from heaven, and speaks of eating His flesh and drinking His blood. Whatever the reading of that passage, it shows that He is the one who feeds, and that life comes only by taking Him in by faith.

Explains why the new covenant involves blood, since a covenant is put into effect by a death. This stands behind the language of the cup in verse 25 and shows that Christ's death is the means of the forgiveness of sins.

The Lord disciplines those He loves, and the discipline is for our good, so that we may share in His holiness. It is the closest commentary on verse 32, where the Lord's judgment on His church is explained as discipline and not condemnation.

Warns of those who are blemishes at the church's love feasts, feasting without fear. It confirms that the problem at Corinth was not a local oddity, and that the shared meal of the early church needed constant care.

Blessed are those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. This is the table that the Lord's Supper anticipates, and it explains why Paul adds until He comes. Each meal at the Lord's table is a foretaste of the great feast.

study.oneStory:
The Supper is a meal in a story that began at a table in a garden. In Eden God gave the man and the woman every tree to eat from freely, Genesis 2:16, and one tree to leave alone. At the fall the human race took food that God had not given, Genesis 3:6, and so a story about eating became a story about death. The rest of Scripture is the story of God setting a table again. At the Passover He feeds His people on the night they are rescued, Exodus 12. At Sinai He seals His covenant with blood and a meal, Exodus 24. In the wilderness He gives manna, and in the land He appoints feasts, so that Israel may remember what He did.

At the climax, on the night He was betrayed, Jesus takes the Passover meal and gives it a new meaning, with Himself as the lamb and the covenant. The church inherits it: the Supper looks back to the cross and tells the world what has happened there, and it looks across at the people beside us, one body, verse 29 with 10:17. It looks forward, too, until He comes, verse 26, to a day when the story of eating is fully mended. Jesus said that He would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until the kingdom of God comes, Luke 22:18, and the book of Revelation shows the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, and the tree of life growing again in the city of God, Revelation 22:2. What was lost at a tree is restored by a Man who died on one, and the feast that follows has no hungry and no humiliated at it.

Corinth's failure fits the story because it is the old fall repeated at the new table: grasping, going ahead, taking one's own. Paul's remedy is the cross, where the One who owned everything gave it all away, and the church learns at the table that it is part of a family and not a private club. Until the final supper, each meal is a small rehearsal of the end, a place where the fractured race is brought back to one table by the same Lord.

quiz.q: Why did Paul say the Corinthians' gatherings did more harm than good?

options.text: Their divisions meant the rich ate their fill while the poor were shamed and went hungry.
options.note: Verses 21 and 22: they humiliated those who had nothing.

options.text: They were using the wrong bread and cup for the meal.
options.note: The problem was not the elements but the loveless, divisive way they ate.

options.text: They had stopped meeting together altogether.
options.note: They did come together; the failure was how they came together.

options.text: They were persecuted by outsiders during the meal.
options.note: The harm came from within, from their own contempt for the poor.

quiz.q: What does the cup represent according to the words of institution?

options.text: The new covenant in Christ's blood, poured out for us.
options.note: Verse 25: this cup is the new covenant in My blood.

options.text: A pledge of the believer's own effort and devotion.
options.note: It is grounded in Christ's blood, not our devotion, though it calls for faith.

options.text: Merely a symbol of fellowship among members.
options.note: It does bind believers together, but its heart is Christ's blood and the covenant.

options.text: The wisdom of God given to the mature.
options.note: That belongs to earlier chapters; the cup proclaims the new covenant in His blood.

quiz.q: What does the Supper proclaim, and for how long?

options.text: The Lord's death, until He comes again.
options.note: Verse 26 sets the Supper between the cross and the return of Christ.

options.text: The Lord's resurrection, until the end of the age.
options.note: The resurrection is our hope, but Paul says the meal proclaims His death until He comes.

options.text: The unity of the local church, for the present generation.
options.note: Unity matters, but the meal proclaims Christ's death, not merely our unity.

options.text: The forgiveness of a single past sin, once for all.
options.note: It proclaims His atoning death continually until He returns.

quiz.q: What is a believer to do before eating and drinking?

options.text: Examine himself and discern the body, coming in repentance and love.
options.note: Verses 28 and 29 call for self-examination and discerning the body.

options.text: Prove himself worthy by being free of all sin.
options.note: The table is for repentant sinners; the call is to examine, not to be sinless.

options.text: Wait to be judged first by the church leaders.
options.note: Paul calls for self-judgment, not clearance by leaders, though love for the body matters.

options.text: Nothing; the meal works regardless of the heart.
options.note: Careless eating brings judgment; the heart and the body must be discerned.

quiz.q: How should we understand the weakness, sickness, and deaths among them?

options.text: As the Lord's fatherly discipline, so they would not be condemned with the world.
options.note: Verse 32: being judged by the Lord is discipline, not condemnation.

options.text: As proof that God had abandoned the whole church.
options.note: It was corrective discipline of His own people, not abandonment.

options.text: As random misfortune with no connection to the Supper.
options.note: Paul directly links it to their abuse of the table, as discipline.

options.text: As final condemnation from which there is no return.
options.note: The point is the opposite: discipline now so they are not condemned later.

questions: The Corinthians turned a meal of grace into a display of status. Where might pride or partiality be quietly shaping how your church, or your table, treats those with less?
The Supper proclaims the Lord's death until He comes. How does holding both the cross behind us and Christ's return before us shape the way you take communion?
Paul says to examine yourself before you eat. What would honest self-examination look like for you the next time you come to the Lord's table?
To discern the body is to see fellow believers as Christ's own. Who in your congregation is easy to overlook, and how could you honor them as part of the body?
God disciplined the church as a Father so they would not be condemned with the world. How does seeing hardship as possible fatherly correction change the way you respond to it?

translationNotes.note: In remembrance of Me translates anamnesis, a covenant memorial rather than mere recollection; the meal proclaims and applies Christ's finished death, echoing how Israel remembered the Passover deliverance.
The new covenant in My blood renders diatheke, covenant, tying the cup to Jeremiah 31 and the blood of the covenant at Sinai; the Supper seals the new and better covenant in Christ's blood.

Without recognizing the body translates diakrino, to discern or distinguish; the phrase can point to discerning the meaning of Christ's body and blood, to discerning the church as His body, or to both together.
